name: intro_body
text:
Optical inspection benefits from reconstruction when clearer boundaries produce more stable position measurements. Changing magnification changes object-space sampling and the pixel phase of the same motion. Single-step displacement dispersion therefore provides a direct test of measurement utility.

MOSR reconstructs each monochrome image on its original pixel grid. One fixed set of learned weights serves 20× and 50× objectives. Raw, fixed Wiener and MOSR use the same image pairs and pillar identities.

name: methods_body
text:
Reconstruction. MOSR combines U-Net context [1], anti-aliasing [2] and bounded PSF-guided correction. The learned weights remain fixed across objectives. Optical inputs comprise 25 measured kernels at 20× and one calibrated kernel at 50×.

Localization. Coarse contours [3] initialize geometric least-squares circle (LSC) centers [4]. The common reader refines each pillar with 720 uniform radial directions, 0.05-pixel profile sampling and three center updates.

Displacement. Each image pair yields nine independent horizontal center shifts. After conversion to object space, their absolute median defines one single-step displacement. The same procedure applies to all three image methods.

name: conclusions_body
text:
MOSR lowers single-step dispersion in every tested condition, with reductions of 9.8–24.1% relative to Raw. The mean condition-level Step SD decreases by 19.5%.

One set of reconstruction weights supports both objectives. Clearer pillar boundaries and lower displacement dispersion establish MOSR as a measurement-oriented reconstruction approach for cross-magnification optical inspection.
